screens.title: Simulation with ModelSim and Quartus Prime Simulator
screens.narratorSegment: Simulation is the safety net you use before placing logic onto an FPGA. In this lesson we focus on two simulators integrated with Quartus Prime: ModelSim‑Intel FPGA for full-featured verification, and the built‑in Quartus Prime Simulator for fast functional checks. You will learn how to launch ModelSim from Quartus, prepare testbenches, add signals to the waveform, and use the Vector Waveform File editor when a quick visual input is enough. We will also cover waveform analysis techniques, how to pause and inspect design state with breakpoints, and common mistakes that produce unknown values or timing glitches. A concrete example will be the lab activity: simulate the 4‑bit sequence detector from Chapter 4.3, add internal state signals to the waveform, measure the delay between input and detected output, and save your waveform as a reusable script. By the end you will know when to pick ModelSim for deep verification and when the Quartus Simulator is enough for a quick check. Consider why a self‑checking testbench speeds regression testing compared with manual waveform inspection.

screens.title: Why simulation is essential
screens.narratorSegment: Simulation is the primary verification step in FPGA design because it lets you observe internal signals and timing without risking hardware. That claim matters: hardware programming hides internal state, but simulation exposes every register, net, and transition. A concrete example is an FSM that mis‑initializes its state register. On silicon, that bug might cause hours of debugging. In simulation you can add the state register to the waveform, step clocks, and immediately see the incorrect initial value. A common misconception is that synthesis will behave exactly like simulation; while synthesis tools aim to preserve behavior, simulation helps catch issues such as uninitialized registers, missing sensitivity list entries in combinational code, or incorrect clock/reset sequencing. For practice, always initialize important registers in your testbench or through reset logic and verify the reset sequence separates from clock edges. Takeaway: use simulation to make internal behavior visible, and treat it as a faster, safer way to validate design assumptions before you ever touch the device. How will you confirm your reset and initialization assumptions in your next project? Why simulation is essential means expose internal states and timing to find logic errors early and save time compared to debugging on hardware.. In practical terms, detect logic and timing bugs before hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Why simulation is essential
Definition and importance
Simulation makes internal nets and state visible so you can verify functional and temporal behavior before hardware.
Detect initialization bugs by observing register values at reset.
Find missing signals in sensitivity lists that block combinational updates.
Measure the timing between input events and output response to validate latency.
Example
A misinitialized FSM state shows as 'X' or an unexpected state in simulation; fix by initializing in reset logic.
Misconception
Synthesis doesn't guarantee you won't see simulation-only issues. Simulation finds issues that synthesis may hide until runtime.
Key Takeaway

Simulate early and often. Validate initialization, reset timing, and combinational logic before hardware testing.

Practical checks to run now
  • Initialize registers in the testbench or assert reset for several clock cycles.
  • Verify clock toggles and reset transitions do not overlap the same edge to avoid ambiguity.
  • Use waveform measurements to confirm outputs assert for the intended number of cycles.
Try this
Add the state register from the sequence detector to your waveform and step the clock to watch transitions happen exactly on the rising edge.

screens.title: ModelSim‑Intel FPGA overview
screens.narratorSegment: ModelSim is the industry‑standard HDL simulator that supports Verilog, VHDL, and mixed‑language projects. It is optimized in the ModelSim‑Intel FPGA edition for Intel device libraries and integrates tightly with Quartus Prime. Key capabilities you will use include advanced waveform analysis, breakpoints to pause execution at a code line, signal tracing to follow dataflow, and code coverage metrics for thorough verification. A concrete example: a self‑checking testbench in ModelSim can assert expected outputs while driving inputs and report pass or fail automatically; this is far more reliable than visual inspection. One misconception is that ModelSim is only for big projects; in practice, it scales from small RTL checks to complex system verification and offers features like radix conversion and waveform saving that accelerate repeated tests. When you prepare a testbench, ModelSim will compile and run it when launched from Quartus. The practical payoff is automated regression tests and easier debugging of timing or logical faults. Concrete example
A self‑checking Verilog testbench can assert conditions and print a pass/fail line in the transcript; ModelSim captures that output and lets you pause where failures occur.
Key Takeaway

ModelSim is the tool for automated, deep verification and debugging across languages and mixed designs.

Quick tips
  • Add important internal signals to the waveform early so you can inspect them after each run.
  • Save waveform setups as a .do file to reproduce the same view on future runs.
  • Use $display or $monitor in your testbench to provide human‑readable traces in the Transcript window.

screens.title: Launch ModelSim from Quartus Prime
screens.narratorSegment: Launching ModelSim from Quartus Prime is a repeatable process that reduces manual file handling. First, write and add your testbench file to the Quartus project so the simulator knows your top‑level stimulus. Next, open Assignments, choose Settings, and under EDA Tool Settings select Simulation. Set the tool name to ModelSim‑Intel FPGA and pick the appropriate HDL format for your design. Once configured, use Tools then Run Simulation Tool and choose RTL Simulation. Quartus will call ModelSim, compile the design and testbench, and load the testbench into the ModelSim workspace. A concrete example: if you switch to Verilog format, Quartus will pass Verilog compilation commands to ModelSim and the testbench will appear in the Objects window ready to drag signals into the waveform viewer. A common misconception is that manual compilation is faster—automating the launch ensures consistent compile orders and reduces user error. Takeaway: follow the named menu steps and verify the testbench appears in ModelSim; this repeatable flow is the foundation for automated verification and regression testing. Launch ModelSim from Quartus Prime means add testbench to project, set eda tool settings → simulation to modelsim, then run rtl simulation from tools.. In practical terms, configure eda settings and run rtl simulation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Launch ModelSim
Step-by-step
  1. Add your testbench file to the Quartus project so it is part of the compile context.
  2. Open Assignments → Settings → EDA Tool Settings → Simulation and set the tool to ModelSim‑Intel FPGA.
  3. Choose Verilog or VHDL as the format based on your sources.
  4. Use Tools → Run Simulation Tool → RTL Simulation. Quartus compiles and launches ModelSim automatically.
Pro Tip

Keep testbenches in the project so the compile order remains consistent across runs and between team members.

Visual checklist
Compile success
Quartus compiles and ModelSim will show compiled units in the Objects window.
Testbench loaded
Confirm the testbench appears and you can drag signals into the waveform viewer.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add the testbench to the project or selecting the wrong HDL format prevents ModelSim from compiling the testbench correctly.

screens.title: Preparing a testbench for simulation
screens.narratorSegment: A testbench provides stimulus, clocking, reset sequencing, and checks that validate your design. At minimum, it must drive clocks and resets, apply representative input patterns, and either include assertions or print checks to the transcript. A simple but critical example: initialize all registers in the testbench or assert an explicit reset for several cycles; otherwise, registers may start as unknown and produce 'X' in waveforms. A misconception is that manually drawing inputs in the waveform editor replaces a testbench. For small functional checks, a Vector Waveform File is convenient, but for regression and automated verification you should create a self‑checking testbench in HDL that uses assertions or $display statements. When adding a testbench to Quartus, put it in the project so ModelSim compiles it in the right order. Finally, include internal signals you want to inspect—state registers, counters, and key nets—so you can add them to the waveform viewer and verify transitions. How will you structure your next testbench to be both repeatable and self‑checking? content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Preparing a Testbench
What to include
  • Clock generation that matches your target clock period.
  • Reset sequence that asserts for several cycles and deasserts away from a clock edge.
  • Initialization of registers or explicit reset inside the design.
  • Stimulus vectors that exercise expected and edge cases.
  • Assertions or $display/$monitor statements for automated checking.
Example
A testbench that asserts reset for five cycles, then shifts a pattern into the sequence detector to verify a detected pulse appears for one clock cycle.
Do and don't
Do: Keep testbenches self‑checking and reproducible so they run unattended in regression suites.
Don't: Rely only on manual waveform drawing for complex verification; it is error‑prone and hard to automate.
Concrete checklist
Add clocks, asserts/resets, stimulus sequences, and print statements. Add internal signals to the waveform before running.
Key Takeaway

A repeatable, self‑checking testbench is the backbone of reliable verification and regression testing.

screens.title: Common run commands and .do scripts
screens.narratorSegment: ModelSim accepts interactive commands and script files to control simulation. Two commands you will use frequently are run -all to run until the testbench finishes and run 1000 ns to advance simulation by a fixed time. Saving commands in a. do file lets you reproduce the same run sequence and waveform setup. For example, you can record adding signals to the waveform, set radix displays, and run a timed simulation in one script so every run looks the same. A common misconception is that you must click the waveform UI manually each time; instead save the setup to a. do file so other team members run identical checks. A concrete example. do fragment might include a run command and a transcript print; use these in the lab to save the waveform configuration after you verified state transitions for the sequence detector. Takeaway: script your runs to ensure repeatability, then measure timing with the cursor or scripted checkpoints. How will you use. do scripts to make your verification reproducible? content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Run Commands
Example .do snippets
Use these commands to control simulation timing and reproduce the same waveform view.
# Example do file commands (ModelSim)
# run until testbench completes
run -all

# or run for a measured time
run 1000 ns

# You can also use $display in the testbench to print to the Transcript window
Why script runs?

Scripts make runs repeatable, ensure the same signals and radix settings are loaded, and allow regression suites to execute identical checks without manual steps.

Practical example
After confirming correct state transitions for the sequence detector, save the waveform layout and include a run 1000 ns line in your .do so anyone can reproduce the exact check.
Key Takeaway

Automate runs with .do files to make verification repeatable and shareable across your team.

screens.title: ModelSim waveform viewer features
screens.narratorSegment: The waveform viewer is where you verify signal timing and functional relationships. Key features include zooming to focus on transitions, using cursors to measure the time between two edges, changing radix to decimal, hex, or binary for readability, and grouping signals into buses for compact inspection. A concrete example: if you add the internal state register and the output 'detected' signal to the waveform, change the state display to binary to read the state code while leaving the output in decimal to quickly confirm it asserts as expected. A common misconception is that more signals always improve debugging; in fact, grouping and selective display make it easier to find the event of interest. Save your waveform layout as a. do file to restore the same view across simulations. Takeaway: use the viewer's measurement and radix tools to turn visual patterns into quantitative checks that you can reproduce and share. screens.title: Common simulation mistakes and debugging techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging simulation failures is often about diagnosing patterns. One common root cause is uninitialized signals: in Verilog, registers that are not set default to unknown 'X', so an output stuck at X often means a missing initialization or an always block not assigning the signal. Another frequent issue is clock and reset race conditions—if reset deasserts exactly on a clock edge the result can be ambiguous; ensure reset transitions are non‑overlapping with clock edges. Missing sensitivity list entries in combinational always blocks prevent outputs from updating when inputs change; use @(*) to avoid this class of bug. Blocking versus non‑blocking assignment mistakes cause ordering issues: in sequential always blocks, use non‑blocking assignments to model parallel register updates. A concrete debugging technique: isolate the failing signal, add $display statements showing input values at important times, add breakpoints where state changes, and check whether the clock is toggling in simulation. After discovering the cause, convert manual checks into assertions to prevent regression. Takeaway: focus on initialization, clock/reset sequencing, full sensitivity lists, and proper assignment types when resolving unexpected simulation behavior. Common simulation pitfalls
Uninitialized signals
Registers left uninitialized may appear as 'X'. Initialize in testbench or through reset logic.
Clock/reset race
Ensure reset deasserts away from a clock edge to avoid ambiguous state transitions.
Missing sensitivity list
Use @(*) for combinational blocks to avoid stale outputs when inputs change.
Blocking vs non‑blocking
Use non‑blocking assignments in clocked blocks to model parallel register updates correctly.
Debugging recipe
  1. Confirm the clock toggles and reset timing in simulation.
  2. Initialize suspect signals and rerun; observe if 'X' clears.
  3. Add $display statements to print inputs and state near the failure time.
  4. Set a breakpoint and step to inspect variable values exactly when transitions occur.
Key Takeaway

Systematically check initialization, clock/reset timing, sensitivity lists, and assignment types to find root causes quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Simulation is the safety net you use before placing logic onto an FPGA. In this lesson we focus on two simulators integrated with Quartus Prime: ModelSim‑Intel FPGA for full-featured verification, and the built‑in Quartus Prime Simulator for fast functional checks. You will learn how to launch ModelSim from Quartus, prepare testbenches, add signals to the waveform, and use the Vector Waveform File editor when a quick visual input is enough. We will also cover waveform analysis techniques, how to pause and inspect design state with breakpoints, and common mistakes that produce unknown values or timing glitches. A concrete example will be the lab activity: simulate the 4‑bit sequence detector from Chapter 4.3, add internal state signals to the waveform, measure the delay between input and detected output, and save your waveform as a reusable script. By the end you will know when to pick ModelSim for deep verification and when the Quartus Simulator is enough for a quick check. Consider why a self‑checking testbench speeds regression testing compared with manual waveform inspection.

These objectives define the verification skills you will practice. First, you will set up and run a ModelSim simulation from within Quartus Prime. That means preparing a testbench, configuring EDA settings, and launching the RTL simulation so ModelSim compiles and loads your testbench automatically. Second, you will use the ModelSim waveform viewer to debug designs. You will add internal signals, change radix displays, zoom to edges, and measure the time between transitions to confirm timing. Third, you will run Quartus Prime's built‑in simulator using the Vector Waveform File editor for quick functional checks by drawing input patterns and observing outputs. Finally, you will compare ModelSim and the Quartus Simulator and choose the right tool for a task: ModelSim for deep, self‑checking verification and Quartus for fast, visual checks when a quick answer is sufficient. Each objective focuses on a practical skill you will exercise in the lab, and each maps to a verified competency milestone you can use to confirm readiness.

This screen maps each objective to a hands‑on milestone you can demonstrate. For running ModelSim from Quartus, show that Quartus launches ModelSim, compiles files, and opens the testbench automatically. As a verification step, add a top‑level signal and one internal state to the waveform and confirm they appear. For waveform debugging, prove you can change display radix, measure time between two signal edges, and group signals into a bus. For the Quartus Simulator objective, create a Vector Waveform File, draw a clock and input sequence, run the simulator, and capture the output waveform. For choosing the workflow, run the same small testbench in both tools and note which produced results faster and which offered better debug visibility. Each milestone is practical: it demonstrates the skills you will use in regression testing, performance checks, and when automating verification. Use these steps to verify competency before moving on to the sequence detector lab.

Simulation is the primary verification step in FPGA design because it lets you observe internal signals and timing without risking hardware. That claim matters: hardware programming hides internal state, but simulation exposes every register, net, and transition. A concrete example is an FSM that mis‑initializes its state register. On silicon, that bug might cause hours of debugging. In simulation you can add the state register to the waveform, step clocks, and immediately see the incorrect initial value. A common misconception is that synthesis will behave exactly like simulation; while synthesis tools aim to preserve behavior, simulation helps catch issues such as uninitialized registers, missing sensitivity list entries in combinational code, or incorrect clock/reset sequencing. For practice, always initialize important registers in your testbench or through reset logic and verify the reset sequence separates from clock edges. Takeaway: use simulation to make internal behavior visible, and treat it as a faster, safer way to validate design assumptions before you ever touch the device. How will you confirm your reset and initialization assumptions in your next project? Why simulation is essential means expose internal states and timing to find logic errors early and save time compared to debugging on hardware.. In practical terms, detect logic and timing bugs before hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ModelSim is the industry‑standard HDL simulator that supports Verilog, VHDL, and mixed‑language projects. It is optimized in the ModelSim‑Intel FPGA edition for Intel device libraries and integrates tightly with Quartus Prime. Key capabilities you will use include advanced waveform analysis, breakpoints to pause execution at a code line, signal tracing to follow dataflow, and code coverage metrics for thorough verification. A concrete example: a self‑checking testbench in ModelSim can assert expected outputs while driving inputs and report pass or fail automatically; this is far more reliable than visual inspection. One misconception is that ModelSim is only for big projects; in practice, it scales from small RTL checks to complex system verification and offers features like radix conversion and waveform saving that accelerate repeated tests. When you prepare a testbench, ModelSim will compile and run it when launched from Quartus. The practical payoff is automated regression tests and easier debugging of timing or logical faults. Launching ModelSim from Quartus Prime is a repeatable process that reduces manual file handling. First, write and add your testbench file to the Quartus project so the simulator knows your top‑level stimulus. Next, open Assignments, choose Settings, and under EDA Tool Settings select Simulation. Set the tool name to ModelSim‑Intel FPGA and pick the appropriate HDL format for your design. Once configured, use Tools then Run Simulation Tool and choose RTL Simulation. Quartus will call ModelSim, compile the design and testbench, and load the testbench into the ModelSim workspace. A concrete example: if you switch to Verilog format, Quartus will pass Verilog compilation commands to ModelSim and the testbench will appear in the Objects window ready to drag signals into the waveform viewer. A common misconception is that manual compilation is faster—automating the launch ensures consistent compile orders and reduces user error. At minimum, it must drive clocks and resets, apply representative input patterns, and either include assertions or print checks to the transcript. A simple but critical example: initialize all registers in the testbench or assert an explicit reset for several cycles; otherwise, registers may start as unknown and produce 'X' in waveforms. A misconception is that manually drawing inputs in the waveform editor replaces a testbench. For small functional checks, a Vector Waveform File is convenient, but for regression and automated verification you should create a self‑checking testbench in HDL that uses assertions or $display statements. Key features include zooming to focus on transitions, using cursors to measure the time between two edges, changing radix to decimal, hex, or binary for readability, and grouping signals into buses for compact inspection. Debugging simulation failures is often about diagnosing patterns. One common root cause is uninitialized signals: in Verilog, registers that are not set default to unknown 'X', so an output stuck at X often means a missing initialization or an always block not assigning the signal. Another frequent issue is clock and reset race conditions—if reset deasserts exactly on a clock edge the result can be ambiguous; ensure reset transitions are non‑overlapping with clock edges. Missing sensitivity list entries in combinational always blocks prevent outputs from updating when inputs change; use @(*) to avoid this class of bug. Blocking versus non‑blocking assignment mistakes cause ordering issues: in sequential always blocks, use non‑blocking assignments to model parallel register updates. A concrete debugging technique: isolate the failing signal, add $display statements showing input values at important times, add breakpoints where state changes, and check whether the clock is toggling in simulation. After discovering the cause, convert manual checks into assertions to prevent regression. Takeaway: focus on initialization, clock/reset sequencing, full sensitivity lists, and proper assignment types when resolving unexpected simulation behavior.
